# c. 1950: propellers over the ocean

By 1950 the unit of long-distance travel had changed from days to hours. Four-engined piston airliners crossed the Atlantic in less than a day, and most European capitals lay a few hours from Paris by air. The liners still sailed, but within a decade they would lose the Atlantic to the aeroplane.

## A traveller: Marcel Cerdan, 1949

At 8.05 p.m. on 27 October 1949, Air France Flight 009 left Orly for New York, a Lockheed Constellation carrying thirty-seven passengers and eleven crew [@air-france-flight]. Like every transatlantic airliner of the day it could not cross in one hop; it was due to refuel at Santa Maria in the Azores [@air-france-flight]. Among the passengers were the former world middleweight boxing champion Marcel Cerdan, on his way to join the singer Édith Piaf in New York, and the violinist Ginette Neveu, travelling with her Stradivarius [@air-france-flight].

They never arrived. Shortly before 3 a.m. the pilot reported the airport in sight; the aircraft then flew into a ridge on São Miguel island, 97 km away, killing all forty-eight people on board [@air-france-flight]. Investigators blamed inaccurate navigation and a failure to identify the airport [@air-france-flight]. The crash shows both sides of the new age: Paris and New York had become an overnight journey, but that journey still depended on stopovers, dead reckoning, and luck.

## The maps

![Europe from Paris, c. 1950](/maps/output/europe_1950.png){#fig-europe-1950 fig-alt="Map of Europe with fast patches around airports: western capitals within about six hours of Paris, Moscow more than a day behind the Iron Curtain" aria-describedby="desc-europe-1950"}

::: {#desc-europe-1950}
Air routes turn Europe into a network of fast islands. Most capitals of western Europe lay within about six hours of Paris, and much of the continent within half a day. The Iron Curtain shows as a sharp slowdown: Moscow, reachable in about five and a half hours two decades later, took more than a day.
:::

![The world from Paris, c. 1950](/maps/output/world_1950.png){#fig-world-1950 fig-alt="World map by air from Paris: New York under a day, Rio, Bombay, and Johannesburg about a day and a half, Tokyo and Sydney three to four days" aria-describedby="desc-world-1950"}

::: {#desc-world-1950}
The whole inhabited world now lay within a few days. New York was less than a day away, Rio, Bombay, and Johannesburg about a day and a half, Tokyo and Sydney three to four days, with several refuelling stops on the way.
:::

## Travel times from Paris, c. 1950

| Destination | Fastest journey | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| London, Brussels | about 3 hours | Estimate, by air |
| Lyon | about 3½ hours | Estimate, by air |
| Rome, Madrid | about 5 hours | Estimates |
| Istanbul | about 12 hours | Estimate |
| Cairo | about 14 hours | Estimate |
| New York | about 20 hours | Estimate; piston airliners crossed the Atlantic in 16–17 hours [@liner-transatlantic-crossing], plus refuelling stops |
| Moscow | more than a day | Estimate |
| Bombay, Rio de Janeiro | about 1½ days | Estimates |
| Tokyo | about 3 days | Estimate; by 1959 the fastest scheduled flight took about 31 hours via Anchorage, or 42 via India [@lockheed-l-1649] |
| Sydney | about 4 days | Estimate |

## Conditions on the road

Flying was still a luxury and an adventure. Post-war airliners were pressurized, but long flights meant a string of stops, and passengers were among the first to feel what would later be called jet lag, the upset of crossing several time zones in a few hours [@evolution-commercial-flying], before there were any jets to blame. Regulated fares meant airlines competed on service: meals, sleeper berths, and personal attention [@evolution-commercial-flying].

At sea, the great liners reached their peak just as they became obsolete. In 1952 the SS *United States* crossed the Atlantic in three and a half days, setting the speed record for the crossing [@liner-transatlantic-crossing].

## The effort of the journey

The aeroplane did away with many of the old labours, from finding an inn to changing horses. It needed a common language instead, at least in the cockpit. In 1951 the International Civil Aviation Organization recommended that English be used universally for international radiotelephone communication in the air [@aviation-english].

Keeping in touch still took patience. A telephone call across the Atlantic went by radio, on a service opened in 1927 that handled around 300,000 calls a year [@tat-1]. The first transatlantic telephone cable, TAT-1, was inaugurated only on 25 September 1956; it could carry 35 calls at once, and in its first 24 hours of public service it carried 588 calls between London and the United States [@tat-1].

## Paying the way

Leaving France with money was itself regulated. Exchange controls introduced in 1939 were tightened at the Liberation and codified in 1947, and they stayed in force through the years of reconstruction [@report-no-150]. Travellers could take only set amounts of currency across the border; a decree of 1960 still fixed these 'tolerances', a word that says much about the official view of holidays abroad, and required anything above them to be declared [@summary-arrete-23]. Britain wrote its limit into the passport itself: a page at the back recorded the foreign exchange taken out of the country, a limited sum of sterling, typically £50 in 1955 (about $2,270 today) [@british-passport; @1-1955-2026; @gbp-usd-historical].

Air fares stayed high. For years the standard round trip between New York and Europe cost $711 (about $8,960 today), when $5,000 was a decent annual salary; on 1 May 1952 the airlines introduced a tourist class at $486 round trip (about $6,120) [@shape-things-come; @100-1952-is].

In New York, a new way to pay was being born. In February 1950 Frank McNamara paid for a restaurant meal with a cardboard Diners Club card, the first charge card accepted by many different businesses [@diners-club-international]. Diners Club billed its members at the end of each month and took a 5–7 per cent fee from the restaurant [@diners-club-credit].

## Papers

A ticket to New York was not enough: until France joined the US Visa Waiver Program in July 1989, a French visitor to the United States needed a visa [@visa-waiver-program].

Some journeys also called for a medical paper. The International Certificate of Inoculation and Vaccination, created by the Hague convention on air travel of 1933 and amended in 1944, was confirmed by the World Health Organization's International Sanitary Regulations of 25 May 1951, as proof of vaccination against diseases such as cholera, yellow fever, and smallpox [@icvp].

Passports were still filled in by hand. A British passport of 1955 recorded the holder's height, eye and hair colour and 'special peculiarities', and could add 'accompanied by his wife' and the children [@british-passport]; the wording left no doubt about who was accompanying whom. It also listed the countries for which it was valid: the Commonwealth, the USA, and all of Europe 'including the USSR' [@british-passport].

## Risks

At the time, Flight 009 was the deadliest accident involving the Constellation [@air-france-flight]. Navigating over open ocean to a small island airfield, largely by the crew's own reckoning, left little margin for error [@air-france-flight].

## Who travelled, and how many

After the war, passenger demand surged and airlines were overwhelmed [@evolution-commercial-flying]. In the United States, more people travelled by air than by train for the first time in 1955, and by 1957 airliners had replaced ocean liners as the usual way to cross the Atlantic [@evolution-commercial-flying]. Flying remained mostly for business travellers and the well-off, and in the United States segregated airports kept many Black Americans from flying at all [@evolution-commercial-flying]. When the airlines introduced a cheaper tourist class on 1 May 1952, the first flights were booked solid [@shape-things-come].
